bib.title: WebThinker: Empowering Large Reasoning Models with Deep Research Capability

legacy_report:
SOURCE: WebThinker: Empowering Large Reasoning Models with Deep Research Capability. Xiaoxi Li, Jiajie Jin, Guanting Dong (equal contribution), Hongjin Qian, Yongkang Wu, Ji-Rong Wen, Yutao Zhu, Zhicheng Dou (Renmin University of China, BAAI, Huawei Poisson Lab). Venue: NeurIPS 2025. Printed on page 1: "39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)". arXiv:2504.21776v2, 13 Oct 2025. Code: https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/WebThinker

COVERAGE: Extracted text is 138,250 chars over 41 pages, and all of it was read except the case-study transcript tables (Tables 4-10, about chars 90,000-117,500), which I skimmed through the paper's own summaries in D.1-D.3, and the reference list, which I skimmed. I read the main body, Tables 1-3, Appendices A-F, the instruction templates and the NeurIPS checklist. Extraction was clean. Table text is flat, so I cross-checked the numbers against the prose.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- Claim: WebThinker-32B-RL is the best 32B system on GPQA, GAIA and WebWalkerQA, and it beats the RAG and Search-o1 baselines at the same size. Search-o1 is the autonomous-search baseline.
  number: GPQA 70.7, GAIA 48.5, WebWalkerQA 46.5, against Search-o1-32B 67.2 / 39.8 / 34.1 and QwQ-32B direct 64.1 / 22.3 / 4.3.
  setup: QwQ-32B backbone, Pass@1. A Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge grades the answers. Search is the Bing API with k=10, and pages are fetched with Crawl4AI. Subsets: GPQA Diamond (198 questions), GAIA text-only validation (103), WebWalkerQA test (680).
  quote: "WebThinker-32B-RL 90.7 50.5 78.9 70.7 56.4 50.0 16.7 48.5 58.8 44.6 40.4 46.5" and "Search-o1-32B 84.9 49.5 73.7 67.2 53.8 34.6 16.7 39.8 43.1 35.0 27.1 34.1"
  where: Table 1, p.6

- Claim: On Humanity's Last Exam, WebThinker-32B-RL beats Search-o1 and the other 32B baselines. The paper says it also beats o3-mini (High). OpenAI Deep Research is still far ahead.
  number: HLE average 15.8 (RL) and 13.0 (Base), against Search-o1 10.8, QwQ-32B direct 9.6, o3-mini High 14.0 and OpenAI Deep Research 26.6.
  setup: 500 randomly sampled text-only HLE questions out of 2,500. Pass@1. The o3-mini and OpenAI Deep Research figures are official numbers (†), not rerun by the authors.
  quote: "WebThinker-32B-RL 16.7 25.6 2.0 12.7 18.0 26.7 15.8 15.6 15.8" and "OpenAI Deep Research† - - - - - - - - 26.6"
  where: Table 2, p.7

- Claim: The headline gains over Search-o1 are stated as relative or percentage-point figures, and the intro and results text give different numbers for them. They are not clearly one metric.
  number: Intro: +21.9% on GAIA and +36.2% on HLE. Results: +22.9% on WebWalkerQA and +20.4% on HLE for Base. RL over Base: +8.5% on GAIA and +21.5% on HLE.
  setup: Base is training-free WebThinker-32B-Base. The text does not say whether these are relative or absolute. Table values give GAIA 48.5 vs 39.8 and HLE 15.8 vs 10.8, which are about +21.9% and +46% relative.
  quote: "WebThinker surpasses Search-o1 by 21.9% and 36.2% on the GAIA and HLE datasets, respectively" and "(e.g., +22.9% on WebWalkerQA and +20.4% on HLE, respectively)"
  where: p.2 and p.8

- Claim: On Glaive scientific report generation, WebThinker scores the top overall, narrowly ahead of Gemini Deep Research. Grok3 DeeperSearch and the RAG baselines trail well behind.
  number: Average 8.0 (Base) and 8.1 (RL) against Gemini2.0 Deep Research 7.9, Grok3 DeeperSearch 6.5, RAG-DeepSeek-R1 6.8 and RAG-Qwen2.5-72B 5.9. The text says WebThinker excels in Completeness (8.4) and Thoroughness (8.2).
  setup: Only 30 Glaive test questions. Four criteria scored 1-10 (comprehensiveness, thoroughness, factuality, coherence). The judges are DeepSeek-R1-671B and GPT-4o, averaged. Evaluation is listwise with random order, and citations are ignored. The authors skipped human evaluation because the systems' reports are easy to tell apart.
  quote: "WebThinker-32B-Base 8.4 8.2 7.7 7.8 8.0" / "WebThinker-32B-RL 8.3 8.4 7.7 7.9 8.1" / "Gemini2.0 Deep Research 8.1 8.07.77.7 7.9"
  where: Fig 4 table, p.8, and App B.2 / C.3.2 for the setup

- Claim: Ablation on Deep Web Explorer. Removing the explorer hurts both modes, and removing link clicking alone hurts problem solving.
  number: Problem-solving average 45.4 (full) vs 38.3 without the explorer vs 42.6 without link clicking. Report average 8.1 vs 7.7 without the explorer.
  setup: Table 3, WebThinker-32B-RL on GPQA, GAIA, WebWalkerQA and HLE.
  quote: "w/o Deep Web Explorer 63.6 38.8 38.5 12.0 38.3" and "w/o Link Clicking 69.7 42.7 42.6 15.2 42.6"
  where: Table 3, p.9

- Claim: Ablation on Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft. Removing autonomous drafting causes the largest drop in report quality, and removing check-and-edit mostly damages coherence.
  number: Average 8.1 (full) vs 6.6 without autonomous draft vs 7.7 without check and edit. Coherence 6.9 without check and edit vs 7.9 full.
  setup: Glaive, 30 questions, LLM judges.
  quote: "w/o Auto. Report Draft 6.3 6.4 6.8 7.0 6.6" and "w/o Report Check & Edit 8.1 8.0 7.6 6.9 7.7"
  where: Table 3 right, p.9

- Claim: Ablation on RL training. Iterative online DPO beats offline DPO and the untrained base on problem solving. It adds almost nothing on report generation.
  number: Problem-solving average 45.4 (RL), 43.2 (offline DPO), 42.1 (Base). Report average 8.1 (RL) vs 8.0 (Base).
  setup: 2 iterations of online DPO, max sequence length 32,768. Training uses about 3k questions sampled from SuperGPQA, WebWalkerQA Silver, OpenThoughts, NaturalReasoning, NuminaMath and Glaive. Only questions QwQ-32B fails by direct generation are kept, and 3 WebThinker-Base responses are sampled per question. For Glaive, 1.5k questions per iteration. Preferences are ranked in order: correctness or report quality, then fewer tool calls, then shorter output beyond a length-ratio threshold γ>1.
  quote: "WebThinker-32B-RL 70.7 48.5 46.5 15.8 45.4", "w/ Offline DPO 69.2 45.6 44.0 14.2 43.2", "w/o Training (Base) 68.7 44.7 41.9 13.0 42.1". Text also says: "Its impact on report generation is minimal, as the base framework is already effective."
  where: Table 3 p.9, Sec 3.5 p.5, App B.1

- Claim: The method works on smaller DeepSeek-R1-distill backbones. It needs a cold-start SFT stage before RL.
  number: WebThinker-R1-7B gains 174.4% (GAIA) and 422.6% (WebWalkerQA) relative to direct generation, and 82.9% and 161.3% relative to standard RAG. Cold-start SFT uses 7.8k trajectories.
  setup: R1-distill 7B, 14B and 32B. Trajectories come from QwQ-32B WebThinker.
  quote: "cold-start SFT (using 7.8k trajectories from QwQ-32B WebThinker)" and "WebThinker-R1-7B achieved relative gains of 174.4% (GAIA) and 422.6% (WebWalkerQA) over direct generation"
  where: Sec 4.6, p.8

- Claim: Predefined RAG workflows help on web-navigation tasks but do not match autonomous search. Query planning and iterative RAG give inconsistent gains on HLE.
  number: WebWalkerQA: RAG-QwQ-32B 31.2, w/ Query Planning 32.5, w/ Iterative RAG 31.5. GAIA: 32.0, 32.0, 35.0.
  setup: Same QwQ-32B backbone.
  quote: "RAG improves performance on these tasks but shows inconsistent gains on complex HLE tasks that require deep integration of reasoning and search."
  where: Table 1 and Sec 4.4, pp.6-8

- Claim: Architecture facts. Search calls trigger the Deep Web Explorer. The explorer is a sub-LRM loop of search and link click that returns a concise "Final Information" block. Reports are written by a separate assistant LLM, so the main LRM never holds the full report text. Check returns only an outline, and every explored page goes into a document memory the writer retrieves from.
  number: none (design).
  setup: Assistant models are Qwen2.5-Instruct with the same parameters as the backbone. Generation max is 81,920 tokens, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20.
  quote: "This avoids injecting the full report text, which could disrupt the reasoning flow." and "These tools are implemented by an assistant LLM, separating the complex task orchestration performed by the main LRM from the detailed text manipulation required for report writing."
  where: App A.1 p.17, Sec 3.4 p.5

LIMITS
- Authors concede: no multimodal input (images and video), only a limited tool set, and no GUI-based web exploration. These are in the conclusion, p.9.
- No error bars, from the checklist: "Due to the high computational cost of our experiments, we did not report error bars." Single-run Pass@1.
- The report evaluation covers only 30 Glaive questions and uses LLM judges only, with no human evaluation. Citations are explicitly excluded from scoring, so citation accuracy is untested. The 8.0 vs 7.9 gap against Gemini is tiny. Glaive questions come from a synthetic dataset generated by DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, not real research tasks. Training uses Glaive too, so train and test share a distribution.
- OpenAI Deep Research is far ahead where it is reported: GAIA 67.4 vs 48.5, HLE 26.6 vs 15.8. The paper's "outperforms proprietary systems" claim holds on Glaive only against Grok3 and Gemini, judged by an LLM.
- Text and table mismatch: Sec 4.7 says "Avg. 44.9 vs 42.1 Base" but Table 3 shows 45.4 for the RL model. Use 45.4.
- The percentage claims mix relative and absolute (see claim 3). Baseline results come from the authors' own reruns, apart from the † figures.
- Search depends on the Bing API and Crawl4AI. The paper reports no cost, latency or tool-call counts, even though training rewards fewer tool calls.
- The 2025 comparisons (QwQ-32B, o3-mini, Grok3 and Gemini 2.0 Deep Research) have dated.

BUILDS ON
Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025, ref [26]; the closest baseline: agentic RAG with a Reason-in-Documents module). Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024). DPO and online or iterative DPO (refs [40], [57], [5]; [5] is Dong et al.). QwQ-32B (Qwen) and DeepSeek-R1 as backbones. CoT (Wei et al. [55]). Benchmarks: GPQA [41], GAIA [32], WebWalkerQA [56], HLE [37], Glaive [11]. RL-with-search work such as ReSearch [2] is cited, but the paper says those methods are Wikipedia-QA focused.

CODE
None as code. The tool protocol tokens are worth keeping (App A.1, p.17): `<|begin_search_query|>` ... `<|end_search_query|>`, `<|begin_search_result|>`, `<|begin_click_link|>`, `<|begin_write_section|> section_name\ncontents_to_write <|end_write_section|>`, `<|begin_check_article|>`, `<|begin_edit_article|> edit_instruction <|end_edit_article|>`. DPO loss is Eq. 6, p.6. The preference priority is correctness, then fewer tool calls, then shorter length (Sec 3.5).

FIGURES
- Fig 2, p.3: standard RAG, iterative RAG with a predefined workflow, and WebThinker's tools inside one continuous thinking process. This is the clearest picture of why it is "agentic".
- Fig 3, p.4: framework overview with the two modes (problem-solving and report generation), the Deep Web Explorer, the document memory, and the write, check and edit tools.
- Fig 4, p.8: Glaive scores table, plus a t-SNE showing broader topic coverage (qualitative only).
- Fig 5, p.8: results on 7B, 14B and 32B R1 backbones against direct generation and standard RAG.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- Bar charts in Fig 1 extracted as loose numbers. I used Tables 1-3 instead.
- Table cells are flattened, with some merged tokens such as "8.07.77.7", which I read as 8.0 / 7.7 / 7.7.
- Case-study tables 4-10 were not read line by line.
